title: Observability-driven deployment recommendation for POC
body:
Context:
This note captures the outcomes of the Nov 12th POC workshop with the Fintech POC team (approx. 12 engineers + SEs). The problem statement: customer wants a high-throughput customer-facing summarization endpoint with strict P95 latency SLO (<= 350ms regionally), strong auditability for a subset of traffic, and cost predictability for production rollouts. We used observability signals (latency distribution, cache hit rate, request fanout) as the decision driver for hosted vs dedicated vs private options.

Why observability-first?
- The customer’s acceptance criteria are operational (latency at load, tail behavior under invoiceable bursts, and ability to detect regressions in quality quickly).
- Instrumentation and tracing gaps are the most common root cause for incident-to-resolution slowness in previous POCs.
- Choosing the deployment mode without clear observability requirements increases drift (undetected QoS regressions) after cutover.

High-level conclusion (recommendation summary):
- Primary: Start POC on Hosted API to validate request patterns, synthetic latency profiles, and KV cache behavior quickly.
- Secondary: Provision a Dedicated warm pool (reserved capacity) for realistic soak testing and for burst handling where P95 must be stable under production load.
- Sensitive subset: Mirror sensitive/regulatory traffic to a Private deployment (VPC) for audit and full request-level observability. Do not route production requests to Private until the POC proves performance parity.
Rationale: Hosted provides fastest iteration and the platform-level telemetry needed to map traffic to tail-latency causes. Dedicated gives predictable token economics and smoothing for production-like throughput. Private is reserved for blueprints where data residency or full-control telemetry (HSM/KMS integrations, SIEM hooks) are mandatory.

Observability metrics driving decisions (minimum suggested):
- P95 and P99 server-side token latency (ms) per route (critical).
- Tail percentiles for first-byte (TTFB) and final token emission.
- KV/prefix cache hit rate and correlated per-request cost delta.
- Median and 95th percent CPU/GPU utilization per model variant.
- Token throughput (tokens/s) and tokens per second per worker.
- End-to-end request trace duration (including pre/post-processing).
- Error rates by class (rate limit, memory OOM, model fallback hits).
- Model output quality metrics (per-prompt BLEU/ROUGE proxies or human eval hooks) sampled nightly.

Decision matrix (workshop synthesis):
- Hosted:
  - Pros: fastest setup, full platform telemetry, cost benchmarking, built-in fallbacks and routing.
  - Cons: less isolation, limited customer-managed KMS, shared noisy neighbors at scale.
  - When: earliest validation, performance benchmarking, synthetic/alpha traffic.
- Dedicated:
  - Pros: predictable throughput, contractual SLAs, capacity isolation for heavy-tail workloads.
  - Cons: commit sizing complexity, potential over/under-provisioning during POC.
  - When: capacity soak test, latency SLO verification at scale, customer pre-prod stage.
- Private:
  - Pros: full network control, KMS/HSM integration, SIEM and compliance hooks, on-prem option for air-gapped.
  - Cons: longer lead time, ops handover, slimmer default telemetry out-of-the-box (customer must onboard tracing sinks).
  - When: regulated traffic requiring data locality or integration with customer security tooling.

Recommended deployment topology for this POC (observability-first hybrid):
Phase 0 (day 0–5): Hosted-only smoke tests
- Deploy model on Hosted with tracing enabled.
- Synthetic traffic profiles: low/medium/high token length and concurrency.
- Key checks: P95 < 350ms for synthetic low-latency path, cache-hit baseline measured, and trace sampling end-to-end validated.
- Deliverable: hosted-observability-baseline dashboard and anomaly rules.

Phase 1 (day 6–18): Canary + Dedicated warm pool
- Enable a small percentage (5–10%) of real traffic to Dedicated warm pool via routing policy.
- Instrument route-level telemetry and compare Hosted vs Dedicated P95/P99 and cost per 1M tokens.
- Run 24-hour soak with elevated concurrency to reveal tail behavior.
- Deliverable: dedicated-vs-hosted comparison report, capacity delta estimate, suggested autoscale policy.

Phase 2 (day 19–30): Private mirror for sensitive traffic, parallel soak
- Mirror (not route) the sensitive traffic to Private environment for audit and SIEM ingest. No user-visible cutover.
- Validate KMS/HSM key rotation, audit log completeness, and metric parity with Hosted/Dedicated.
- Deliverable: private-audit-playbook + go/no-go checklist for production migration.

Phase 3 (post-POC): Cutover plan and runbook
- If Dedicated meets SLOs and cost targets, recommend Dedicated primary with Hosted fallback routes for overflow.
- If regulatory constraints require, migrate sensitive routes to Private and maintain Dedicated for general traffic.
- Establish rollback policies and automated routing fallbacks (hosted->dedicated->hosted) with health checks.

Observability runbook (concrete checks to implement during POC):
- Trace sampling: 100% sampling for synthetic tests, 10% for production-candidate traffic, 100% sampling for mirrored sensitive traffic in Private.
- Correlation ids: ensure SDK injects x-rdw-cid for every request. Add uniform span naming: model.infer, model.kv_lookup, model.token_emit.
- Dashboards: per-route latency histogram, cache-hit rate, model-fallback-rate, GPU util, and error taxonomy.
- Alerts: P95 > 350ms sustained for 5 minutes, P99 > 700ms, cache hit drop > 10% vs baseline.
- Regression detection: daily quality delta > threshold triggers evaluation job and a human review.

Capacity sizing worked example (customer expected 1k qps peak, average 200 tokens per request):
- Baseline token rate = 1k * 200 = 200k tokens/s peak.
- Assume per-GPU steady tokens/s = 10k (quantized model estimate from prior benchmarks) => require 20 GPUs for peak.
- Dedicated warm pool recommendation: 25 GPUs (20 active + 5 buffer for headroom / autoscale).
- Hosted baseline for initial POC: 5–8 instances to capture request diversity and cache hit behavior.
Notes: these are rough estimates to be refined after hosted baseline telemetry.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Observability blind spots in Private environment (missing traces). Mitigation: user acceptance criteria includes trace parity; implement CI job that verifies spans and logs on deployment.
- Risk: Cost blowouts during soak. Mitigation: budget caps on Dedicated and rate-limiting on hosted CDS routes.
- Risk: Tail latency due to cold KV cache. Mitigation: pre-warm set of popular prefixes and enable continuous prefix caching for warm pool.

Open questions (from workshop):
- Exact list of routes that are "sensitive" (need to be mirrored to Private). Action: product + security to enumerate.
- Customer SIEM ingest format and retention requirement (who owns log archival?). Owner: security.
- Acceptance threshold for model-output quality drift (quant metric or human sampling cadence?). Owner: product.

Action items and owners:
- (Avery) Build hosted-observability-baseline dashboard template and share by 2024-11-20.
- (Maya) Configure trace sampling and x-rdw-cid SDK hooks; validate with synthetic trace-ID chain tests by 2024-11-18.
- (Ravi) Draft Dedicated autoscale policy with buffer sizing and cost estimation by 2024-11-25.
- (Sofia) Coordinate Private mirror setup with customer infra team and run SIEM ingest verification by 2024-12-02.

Appendix: quick checklist for SEs running this POC
- Ensure SDK versions >= 1.3.2 (contains x-rdw-cid and span names).
- Add per-route tags in request metadata: customer_route, sensitivity_level, test_phase.
- Record nightly composite metric: cost_per_1M_tokens, p95_latency, cache_hit_pct.
- Keep a single source-of-truth spreadsheet for capacity numbers and update after each soak.

Summary: prioritize observability during early validation on Hosted, use Dedicated to verify production-scale SLOs and economics, and reserve Private for mirrored sensitive traffic and final compliance checks. The hybrid, metrics-driven sequence reduces risk and keeps the customer in an iterative feedback loop while preserving options for deterministic cutover.
